prompt: Write a ~700-word piece of literary short fiction about: a night ferry that takes no passengers. Prose only, no headings.
text:
The harbor mist clung to the water like wet wool, heavy and smelling of diesel fuel and salt decay, but tonight it was different; the air carried something thinner, sharper, as if the world above had been scrubbed clean by a sudden, unnatural wind. The *Silent Meridian* sat at its dock, not bobbing restlessly in the chop, but anchored with an eerie stillness that defied the usual lurch of engine idling and hull flexing. Its lights were dimmed to a mournful amber, casting long, distorted shadows across the empty wharf where crates rattled softly against each other in the wind alone. There was no crew visible on deck, only the faint suggestion of movement behind frosted glass windows that seemed to look out rather than in.

I stood at the edge of the pier, my breath pluming into the cold air despite wearing three layers, compelled by a gravity I could not name to step onto the gangplank. The iron stairs groaned under my weight, but there was no one else waiting for me. No ticket booth, no conductor shouting over the roar of unseen engines, just the rhythmic *click-clack* of heels against metal and the distant cry of a gull that sounded suspiciously human in its phrasing. As I climbed aboard, the air inside changed instantly from biting cold to a sterile, room-temperature chill, smelling faintly of ozone and old books. The corridors were lined with plush velvet seats arranged in neat rows, all empty save for me.

The ferry did not move immediately; it hovered on the threshold between departure and arrival, suspended in that liminal state where physics seemed merely to be waiting for permission to resume its duties. Slowly, imperceptibly at first, the water outside began to swirl, then pull away as if gravity had decided to release its hold entirely before reclaiming it a moment later. We moved forward into the darkness of open sea, yet there were no waves breaking against the hull, only a smooth, glassy reflection that mirrored nothing but our own solitary vessel cutting through an ocean made of ink and stars too bright for mortal eyes.

Inside the cabin below deck, which I discovered by pressing my hand against a wall panel until it yielded silently, lay rows of identical beds with white sheets folded to military precision. Each bed held no sleeper, yet there was warmth in them, as if someone had just left them. On small nightstands sat glasses half-filled with water that didn't slosh when I moved the tray, and books open on pages that shifted text whenever I glanced down for more than a second. It felt less like abandonment and more like a rehearsal space where actors have forgotten their lines but kept the stage set perfectly in place while waiting for the curtain to rise again.

As night deepened into something resembling twilight from another dimension, the silence inside grew deafening. It was not an absence of sound so much as the presence of a profound listening; every creak of timber and whisper of wind felt amplified, monitored by invisible ears that judged my heartbeat against some internal rhythm. I realized with a jolt that this ferry never left port because it could never reach its destination in time for anyone else to board or disembark. It traveled only when the world above was asleep enough not to notice, carrying passengers who had already died of old age before they took their first breath on land, bringing them back one more trip so they might see what a life truly looks like from the other side without regret interrupting the view.

The journey felt infinite yet instantaneous, stretching hours in my mind while lasting mere seconds physically. I watched through portholes that offered views of underwater cities built by bioluminescent flora and schools of fish with eyes human-sized, swimming past structures of coral glass where light refracted into colors words had never possessed before now. There was no fear here, only a strange sense of being exactly where one belonged despite having nowhere to be going next. The ferry glided on currents that ran beneath the surface of reality itself, taking us through layers of existence we usually skimmed over in our daily rush.

Finally, as dawn broke not with golden rays but with a soft violet hue filtering through thick clouds above an ocean floor now visible like a starlit ceiling, I found myself at the bow looking down into waters that reflected skies from ages past and future simultaneously. The boat stopped moving, hovering just above the seabed where time seemed to have pooled stagnant and slow enough for thought to take root without rushing toward conclusion or end. And then, as if waking from a dream one never wishes fully remembered, I stepped off onto solid ground again on the shore of my own life, alone once more but carrying within me the quiet knowledge that no matter how lonely we feel standing at docks waiting for rides that don't come or cars that stall in traffic jams nobody else can see, there is always a vessel moving somewhere through dimensions unseen, taking everyone exactly where they need to go before anyone realizes they are missing.
topic: a night ferry that takes no passengers
